stem.text: How might an increase in the surplus on the current account of the balance of payments affect other macroeconomic objectives in the short run?

options.text: by increasing the rate of inflation

explanation.text: A larger current account surplus means net exports (exports minus imports) have risen, which is itself an increase in a component of aggregate demand. In the short run, this higher aggregate demand tends to raise the price level — i.e. increase the rate of inflation — alongside raising output and employment (since AD is rising, not falling).

optionAnalysis.text: A rising net export component of AD tends to increase, not decrease, economic growth in the short run, since it is an increase in demand.
Higher AD from rising net exports tends to increase, not decrease, employment, as firms respond to higher demand by producing (and hiring) more.
Sustainable development is a long-run, structural concept (about preserving resources for future growth) and is not a short-run consequence of a change in the current account balance.
The rise in net exports increases aggregate demand, which in the short run can push the price level up — i.e. raises the rate of inflation, a trade-off against the balance of payments objective.

reasoningChain: Recall that net exports are a component of aggregate demand (AD = C + I + G + (X−M)).
An increased current account surplus means X−M has risen, raising AD.
In the short run (with the economy not necessarily at full capacity but demand rising), higher AD tends to raise both real output and the price level.
Match the price-level effect to 'increasing the rate of inflation', recognising this is a trade-off against the price-stability objective even as the external position improves.

inferredMistakes.text: Assuming an improving current account automatically means other indicators move favourably too, without separately tracing through that the underlying cause (rising net exports/AD) is actually inflationary in the short run.
